title: Paloma and the Winter
premise: Hospice nurse Ansel Amberdale has spent years keeping patients at arm's length, but the dying at Hollowmere House all count backwards in their sleep—and his overnight audio recordings keep catching a second voice asking them questions. When the recordings begin answering questions about Ansel himself, he realizes the voice is cataloguing him, learning the shape of his forgotten childhood the way frost learns a window. To survive the winter, Ansel must recover the song his mother sang—the one whose last verse was never taught to him—and finish it without joining in, because the voice can only take what answers. In the end, Ansel chooses to sing the verse aloud, trading his memories of belonging for the lives of his patients, and walks out of Hollowmere unable to remember why he ever came.
about_author: Lena Okafor is a former night-shift caregiver who writes horror about the hours between three and five in the morning. She lives in a drafty coastal town where she collects lullabies and refuses to record herself humming.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Ansel, POV, begins a winter posting at Hollowmere House and notices his dying patients all count backwards in their sleep—down from different numbers, always reaching zero at dawn. He records the rooms out of clinical habit. Emotional beat: professional detachment established, first crack of unease.

chapters.title: Second Voice
chapters.summary: Ansel, POV, listens back to the recordings and hears a low, patient voice asking each sleeper questions—names, dates, a street he half-remembers. The patients answer in their sleep, gladly. He tells himself it's cross-talk between rooms. Emotional beat: denial hardening into obsession.

chapters.title: What the Frost Knows
chapters.summary: Ansel, POV; the voice begins asking questions about him—his mother, a kitchen, a song. Frost patterns on the windows spell fragments he almost recognizes. A patient wakes screaming that 'it already has your half.' Emotional beat: the horror turns inward.

chapters.title: Marisol's Ledger
chapters.summary: Marisol, a night aide who has survived three winters at Hollowmere, POV; she shows Ansel her ledger of every patient who 'went at zero' and warns him never to answer aloud after dark. She recognizes the song from her grandmother's funeral. Emotional beat: reluctant alliance, first real fear.

chapters.title: The Kitchen in the Recording
chapters.summary: Ansel, POV; a recording captures his own sleeping voice describing his mother's kitchen in detail he doesn't consciously possess. Digging through a box of his late mother's things, he finds sheet music missing its final page. Emotional beat: memory as unreliable shelter, grief surfacing.

chapters.title: Zero at Dawn
chapters.summary: Marisol, POV; a beloved patient reaches zero at dawn and the room's frost forms a perfect portrait of Ansel as a child. Marisol burns the recording and half the ledger, and admits the voice took her sister decades ago. Emotional beat: loyalty to Ansel vs. the truth she's hidden.

chapters.title: The Verse That Wasn't Taught
chapters.summary: Ansel, POV; the voice, now audible while he's awake, offers him a bargain: it will spare the patients if he answers one question honestly. He realizes his mother cut off the song's last verse to keep something from answering her. Emotional beat: the choice between forgetting and belonging crystallizes.

chapters.title: Every Bed Counts Down
chapters.summary: Ansel and Marisol, alternating POV; all nine remaining patients begin counting backwards simultaneously, and the house's frost closes the exits. The voice asks Ansel his question: 'Who sang you to sleep?' He almost answers. Emotional beat: siege, sacrifice, the temptation of surrender.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Ansel, POV, climax; in the frost-locked ward he reconstructs the final verse from the patients' counting—it was a lullaby of farewell all along. He sings it aloud, alone, refusing to answer the question even as the voice sings along inside his mouth. Emotional beat: courage as self-erasure.

chapters.title: Spring, Mostly
chapters.summary: Marisol, POV, resolution; the patients wake counting upwards, the frost melts, and Ansel packs his car with no memory of why he came or why Marisol cries saying goodbye. On the dashboard lies a completed page of sheet music in his handwriting. Emotional beat: bittersweet release—belonging traded away, loyalty remembered only by the one left behind.
